original_question: Prove or disprove that for every integer k greater than 2, the Diophantine equation y = 2 x1 x2 ... xk + 1 has infinitely many solutions in prime numbers. Also determine whether the positive integers can be partitioned into infinitely many arbitrary classes so that at least one class contains an arithmetic progression of l terms with l greater than 3, and find the largest such l.
target_in_paper: Sections 2.3 and 2.4 of Section 2, "Unsolved Problems in Mathematics": the §2.3 conjecture titled "Diophantine equation" and the immediately following §2.4 open problem titled "Van der Waerden theorem."
correct_elements: Your draft correctly identifies the two adjacent mathematical open problems actually stated in the paper: first, the §2.3 conjecture that for each integer k>2 the equation y=2x1x2...xk+1 should have infinitely many solutions in primes; second, the §2.4 question about partitioning N* into infinitely many classes and asking for the largest progression length l>3 for which one class contains an arithmetic progression of l terms.
missing_details: The draft combines two separate paper items (§2.3 and §2.4); the paper does not present them as a single combined conjecture.
In §2.3, "solutions in primes" should be made explicit as requiring x1,...,xk and y all to be prime numbers.
The quantifier in §2.3 is for each fixed positive integer k>2; that should be stated explicitly.
The paper does not state that the primes x1,...,xk,y must be distinct; a stand-alone formulation should clarify that no distinctness condition is imposed in the paper.
In §2.4, the notation N* is used without definition; a stand-alone version should define it, normally as the set of positive integers.
The phrase "partition into an infinity of arbitrary classes" should be formalized as a countable partition into pairwise disjoint nonempty classes whose union is N*.

The phrase "arbitrary classes" is ambiguous in the paper; to make the question sharp, one must specify whether the statement is intended to hold for every such partition or merely for the existence of one. The van der Waerden context strongly suggests the universal reading.
The phrase "an arithmetic progression of l terms" should be written explicitly as a,a+d,...,a+(l-1)d with d>0.
The second problem asks for the largest such l, if it exists; a complete formulation should allow the outcomes that no such l exists or that there is no finite maximum.
refined_question: For the two open problems posed in §2.3-§2.4 of the paper, determine whether: (i) for each fixed positive integer k>2, the Diophantine equation y=2x1x2...xk+1 has infinitely many solutions with x1,...,xk,y all prime numbers (with no distinctness condition imposed); and (ii) writing N* for the set of positive integers, there exists a largest integer l>3 such that every countable partition N*=⨆_{i=1}^∞ Ci into pairwise disjoint nonempty classes contains at least one class Ci that includes an arithmetic progression a,a+d,...,a+(l-1)d with d>0; if so, find the maximum such l.
justification: The draft is very close to the paper’s wording: its first clause reproduces the conjecture in §2.3, and its second clause reproduces the immediately following open problem in §2.4. Section 2 explicitly says that most of these mathematics problems are taken from reference [16], and the paper does not provide any further theorem, proposition, or equivalent reformulation nearby. The main work needed to make the draft stand-alone is therefore to unpack shorthand and ambiguity: in §2.3, the paper says only that the equation has "solutions in primes," so the primality of all variables must be spelled out; in §2.4, the notation N* and the phrase "arbitrary classes" are left implicit. Because §2.4 is framed as "Expanding to infinity van der Waerden’s theorem," the refined question interprets the partition clause in the natural van der Waerden-style sense as quantifying over all countable partitions, which is the narrowest nontrivial sharpening consistent with the paper’s stated intent.
